title: Iran’s Maritime Threat and the Conflict in Yemen
summary: Iran’s Maritime Threat and the Conflict in Yemen bbert@hudson.org Tue, 10/27/2026 - 16:11 SVG Reports Oct 28, 2026 Hudson Institute Iran’s Maritime Threat and the Conflict in Yemen Can Kasapoğlu Senior Fellow (Nonresident) Can Kasapoğlu Reports Caption A fighter loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government fires a turret from the back of a pickup truck around Mount al-Midan in Yemen’s western Taiz province on October 26, 2026. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute report analyses Iran's maritime threat and the conflict in Yemen.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Iran and its Houthi proxies pose a growing maritime threat that reaches beyond the Strait of Hormuz. They say Tehran has threatened Middle East undersea cables, and that the Red Sea, which carries most Europe-Asia cable capacity, is a consequential target, though Iranian and Houthi seabed-warfare capabilities remain unproven. They also describe a shift in IRGC anti-ship tactics toward engine-room strikes, which can disable ships for months and tighten shipping capacity without a full closure of Hormuz. On Yemen, they assess that Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi targets are causing rising economic disruption, straining air defence stocks, and pulling in other regional states such as Egypt. The piece closes by framing the key question as whether military pressure can cut Houthi launch rates before the damage deepens.
brief.argument: Iran and the Houthis are widening a maritime and economic threat, from undersea cables to engine-room strikes on shipping, while the Yemen war escalates and draws in more regional actors.
recommendations: Build redundancy in regional digital connectivity, including terrestrial and alternative submarine routes, to protect Gulf states' AI and cloud projects
Limit damage to the energy-carrying fleet and restore shipping confidence, not just keep a navigable corridor open
Degrade Houthi launchers and underground facilities to reduce launch rates before economic losses deepen
brief.turkey: The Red Sea cable and shipping risks and the Yemen escalation bear on Türkiye's maritime and Gulf-linked interests, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

title: Serbia Election Marks the End of an Era
summary: The country’s student-led opposition movement secured a historic victory in parliamentary elections. But the new government will have its work cut out, says CFR senior fellow Charles Kupchan.

ai.sum: A student-led opposition movement won a historic victory in Serbia's parliamentary elections, according to Charles Kupchan.

brief.summary: The authors, through an interview with CFR senior fellow Charles Kupchan after his trip to Belgrade, describe Serbia's October 2026 parliamentary election as the end of Aleksandar Vucic's fourteen years in power. They frame the win for the student-led Student List (around 53 percent against roughly 40 percent for Vucic's SNS) as the product of nearly two years of protests sparked by a railway canopy collapse in Novi Sad that protesters blamed on corruption. Kupchan describes a spontaneous civil-society mobilisation, high turnout near 70 percent, and a movement whose slogan was 'Serbia or the mafia'. He argues the central challenge now is converting grassroots momentum into governance, given the movement's lack of a clear leader and its many inexperienced winners. He expects the new government to focus on anti-corruption, purging loyalists and reforming the media and economy, with likely closer EU ties, more distance from Russia, and a possible revival of the Belgrade-Pristina normalisation dialogue.
brief.argument: The election marks the end of the Vucic era, but the student-led movement now faces the harder task of turning protest momentum into effective governance against an entrenched patronage network.
recommendations: Focus the new government on fighting corruption and purging Vucic loyalists from ministries and public enterprises
Open up the media landscape that had been dominated by Vucic
Implement economic reforms and reduce political patronage
Use democratic reform progress to improve relations with the EU and possibly reopen the normalisation dialogue with Kosovo
brief.turkey: A Serbia moving closer to the EU and further from Russia, with a possible revival of the Belgrade-Pristina dialogue, would be a relevant Balkan development for Türkiye's regional diplomacy.

brief.summary: The article argues that Lula's reelection in Brazil's 25 October 2026 runoff, won by about 3.5 points over Flávio Bolsonaro, defies a regional drift toward leaders accommodating Donald Trump. The authors credit a late grassroots mobilisation of progressives and centrists, who were alarmed by the prospect of another Bolsonaro presidency. They stress the campaign's digital strategy, including a WhatsApp channel with about 10 million members that spread concerns about Flávio's pledges to cut social spending, and a campaign built on reactions to perceived tech-platform bias. The piece also notes that Flávio refused to concede, that Trump called the vote 'rigged' after appearing to favour Bolsonaro, and that several right-wing regional leaders nonetheless recognised Lula's win, which the piece reads as a sign of regional autonomy.
brief.argument: Lula's narrow comeback victory came from a last-minute grassroots and digital mobilisation that overcame the right's early advantage and signalled regional resistance to Trump's pressure.

title: Afghanistan: Iran's strategic depth card in Central Asia
summary: Afghanistan: Iran's strategic depth card in Central Asia newspress_en Wed, 10/28/2026 - 03:38 Politics In 1998, Iran was hours away from invading Afghanistan after the Taliban killed 11 senior Iranian diplomats in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif. Iranian General Qasem Soleimani, who led the elite Quds Force for decades, had waged a proxy war against the Pakistani-backed Taliban for much of the 1990s, so he knew it well. Years later, American diplomats confirmed that…

ai.sum: An analysis examines how Iran has used its historical proxy role in Afghanistan as strategic depth in Central Asia.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Iran has turned its relationship with the Taliban into a strategic asset, a marriage of convenience that gives Tehran strategic depth in Central Asia. They trace the arc from the 1998 Mazar-i-Sharif crisis, when Iran nearly invaded, through Qasem Soleimani's proxy war and his covert intelligence cooperation with the United States in 2001. They note that such cooperation is now highly unlikely. The piece says Iran's ties to Kabul have grown as the Taliban has broken with Pakistan, its former patron, and that Russia and China share an interest in an Iran-Afghanistan alignment against American influence. Around 2010, US generals accused Iran of backing the Taliban insurgency, and the authors suggest Tehran and Soleimani outmanoeuvred both the ISI and the CIA. They conclude that Iran's links to al-Qaeda help explain how the two became partners. The text is partial, so the full policy logic is only sketched.
brief.argument: Iran's pragmatic partnership with the Taliban, after decades of enmity, gives Tehran strategic depth in Central Asia within an emerging anti-American alignment.
brief.turkey: A deepening Iran-Taliban alignment, backed by Russia and China, could affect Türkiye's Central Asian and Afghan interests and the Pakistan-Taliban rift that bears on regional connectivity.

brief.summary: The authors argue that crypto platforms are using sports sponsorship, particularly in the Gulf, as a funnel that turns fan attachment into contests, rewards and exclusive experiences, and ultimately into account openings, deposits and trading. Sport offers a large, emotionally engaged audience that conventional financial advertising struggles to reach. They point to the Gulf's expanding sports industry, its hosting of major events, heavy state investment in clubs and broadcasting, and a young, smartphone-heavy population as reasons the region is attractive. They cite the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, Crypto.com's long-running Formula One partnership, and a Chiliz deal with the UAE Pro League involving fantasy games and blockchain-verified collectables. The piece stresses that market-size estimates are indicative only and that viewing figures do not reveal whether fans actually adopted digital wallets or stayed active.
brief.argument: Crypto platforms are using Gulf and global sports sponsorships to convert fan loyalty into financial product sign-ups and trading activity, a pathway that conventional advertising cannot easily replicate.

We have watched these dynamics with specific interest, in discussions with congressional staff over bills and appropriations, and in conversations with our clients.Congress adjourned at…

ai.sum: A War on the Rocks analysis argues the next US Congress must reassert oversight of the Department of Defense against executive overreach.

brief.summary: The authors argue that since January 2025 the Trump administration has expanded executive power over the Department of Defense far beyond precedent, while a Congress that has largely deferred to the president remains quietly able to check it. They contend that the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and the emerging FY27 bill already contain tools to reclaim oversight: funding freezes tied to certifications, consultation requirements with allies, reporting duties on leadership removals and force posture cuts, and mandates favouring alliances, NATO and Indo-Pacific commitments. They say the administration has ignored several of these provisions and signalled it will not follow others, so enforcement depends on Congress using appropriations and oversight. The piece expects a likely Democratic House and possibly Senate after the midterms to be better placed to apply that oversight.
brief.argument: A future Congress must enforce the statutory limits it already wrote into the NDAA, using appropriations and oversight because the executive is ignoring them.
recommendations: Enforce existing NDAA mandates through oversight and funding leverage rather than relying on public confrontation
Require the Department to supply written justifications for troop and command restructuring, including the European posture reviews
Use appropriations to hold back funds until certifications and notifications on leadership removals are provided
Keep allied and NATO consultation requirements and the Western Hemisphere-first posture under congressional review

title: Australia and Japan: Formalizing an Informal Alliance
summary: Australia and Japan: Formalizing an Informal Alliance bbert@hudson.org Tue, 10/27/2026 - 13:49 SVG Reports Oct 28, 2026 Hudson Institute Australia and Japan: Formalizing an Informal Alliance James J. Przystup Senior Fellow, Japan Chair James J. Przystup Reports Caption Japan’s Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Australia’s Defence Minister Richard Marles review honor guards during a welcome ceremony at the Ministry of Defense in Tokyo on December 7, 2025. (Getty Images)…

ai.sum: A Hudson Institute report examines moves to formalise the long-informal security alliance between Australia and Japan, citing defence ministers' meetings.

brief.summary: The authors trace how Australia and Japan moved from an informal security partnership to a formalised one over roughly two decades. They draw on each country's foreign policy, defence and strategic documents, which increasingly describe a deteriorating Indo-Pacific shaped by China's military expansion, North Korean missile development, and gray-zone pressure in the East and South China Seas. The argument rests on converging threat assessments and a steady sequence of institutional steps: the 2003 Memorandum on Defense Exchange, the 2007 Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation, annual ministerial dialogues, equipment and reciprocal access agreements, and the December 2025 Framework for Strategic Defence Coordination. The report also tracks operational integration through exercises such as Talisman Sabre, the Mogami frigate procurement, and coordination on Pacific island development. The authors present this as a deepening relationship moving toward a practical alliance, with the US alliance network remaining central.
brief.argument: Australia and Japan have progressively formalised an informal alliance, driven by shared threat perceptions of China and a deteriorating regional order.

title: Permanently Temporary – Syrian Refugees in Jordan
summary: Between pressure to return and blocked integration

ai.sum: A SWP report says Syrian refugees in Jordan face pressure to return while integration remains blocked.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Jordan, despite generous conditions and substantial donor funding, offers Syrian refugees no durable solution. Resettlement is marginal, voluntary return is unlikely given security, housing and economic obstacles, and local integration is politically blocked by Jordan, which has not signed the Refugee Convention. The result is a compromise of limited, revocable and externally funded participation that lets refugees manage daily life but gives them few rights or prospects. Most work is informal, debt is widespread, and education access does not carry through to secondary or higher education. The authors say the compromise is weakening as donor funding falls and return expectations grow, raising the risk of pressured or involuntary returns. They draw lessons on donor language, the limits of the Jordan Compact, cash-for-work programmes and conditionality, and urge Germany and the EU to protect basic provision, support return as a staged process, and expand complementary mobility routes.
brief.argument: Jordan's interim arrangements for Syrian refugees, built on a compromise between Jordanian government interests and donor priorities, are becoming fragile as funding declines and return pressure grows, without providing durable solutions.
recommendations: Maintain basic provision and protection for refugees so they can live with dignity, since further cuts would deepen poverty and push people toward involuntary return.
Treat return as a staged process with reliable information, go-and-see visits, protection monitoring and reintegration support, with particular attention to women and female-headed households.
Expand complementary mobility options, including transnational and regional labour mobility and education pathways, and remove barriers such as work permit costs and social security debts.
Prioritise support for return from within the region over return from Germany, given Syria's fragile situation.

title: President John F. Kennedy and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev Reach a Deal—Cuban Missile Crisis, Day Thirteen
summary: The United States and the Soviet Union pulled back from the nuclear brink, chastened by their brush with nuclear armageddon.

ai.sum: Kennedy and Khrushchev reached a deal on day thirteen of the Cuban Missile Crisis, pulling both superpowers back from nuclear brink.

brief.summary: The authors recount Day Thirteen of the Cuban Missile Crisis, 28 October 1962, when Khrushchev announced the Soviet Union would dismantle and return the missiles in Cuba. Kennedy welcomed the decision publicly and in a formal reply that also expressed regret over a U-2 that strayed into Soviet airspace. He ordered surveillance flights paused and the naval quarantine not enforced to protect the deal. The piece presents the outcome as the two superpowers stepping back from nuclear war, leading to the 1963 Limited Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. It also notes that Kennedy kept secret his pledge to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey, a detail confirmed only in 1989, and that Castro opposed the withdrawal. The narrative is a historical retrospective drawn from the ExComm record and presidential actions, with no new policy prescriptions.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Kennedy and Khrushchev reached a peaceful settlement on Day Thirteen, with Kennedy protecting the deal by pausing reconnaissance and quarantine enforcement and keeping his Jupiter-missile pledge to Khrushchev secret.
brief.turkey: The piece confirms that Kennedy secretly pledged to remove the Jupiter missiles from Türkiye as part of the settlement, a bargain made without Ankara's visible role and only disclosed decades later.

summary: Ukraine Military Situation Report | October 28 bbert@hudson.org Wed, 10/28/2026 - 11:45 SVG Commentary Oct 28, 2026 Hudson Institute Ukraine Military Situation Report | October 28 Can Kasapoğlu Senior Fellow (Nonresident) Can Kasapoğlu Commentary Caption Ukrainian soldiers inspect forward infantry positions near the border with Russia on August 28, 2026, in Oblast Region, Ukraine. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute published its Ukraine military situation report for October 28 covering the war's battlefield developments.

brief.summary: The authors give a weekly battlefield assessment of the Ukraine war. They argue the front lines stayed largely stable while Russia intensified ballistic missile salvos against Ukrainian cities, and that Ukraine's interception rates against jet-powered drones appear to be improving, though larger datasets are needed to confirm this. Their main focus is Ukraine's Operation Veles, a subterranean campaign fought inside gas pipelines near Kupiansk, aimed at closing a Russian infiltration route beneath the Oskil River. They stress that underground warfare is regaining relevance because drones make surface movement easier to detect, and that control of narrow passages can shape logistics and infiltration over a wider area. Casualty and advance figures cited are official Ukrainian claims the authors note are unverified. They also flag Russia's Filin cruise missile as a potential new strain on Ukrainian air defences if produced at scale.
brief.argument: Ukraine's underground campaign near Kupiansk is an important new front, while Russia's missile campaign and the possible mass production of the Filin cruise missile pose growing pressure on Ukrainian air defences.

title: Middle Powers and the Illusion of a Post-America Middle East
summary: Gulf diplomacy fuels claims of a middle-power moment, but the Iran war exposes limits to strategic autonomy and enduring US supremacy.

ai.sum: A RUSI analysis argues the Iran war exposes limits to Gulf middle-power strategic autonomy and enduring US dominance.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the fashionable idea of a 'middle-power moment' in the Gulf overstates how far states such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar have escaped American primacy. They contend that the perceived US retreat is misread: Washington can cut troop numbers while keeping the bases, intelligence and logistics needed to re-enter crises at scale, as seen in the Islamic State campaign, Gaza and the Iran war. Diversifying partners, they say, is not autonomy, and past episodes such as Cold War bargaining and the 1973 oil embargo show that activism can be performative and non-systemic. They judge the 2026 Mecca collective-defence pact untested in practice, and argue the Iran war exposed Gulf dependence on US missile defence and Western arms supply chains. Still, they see some real movement toward autonomy in domestic arms production in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, which could make diplomatic reach more durable.
brief.argument: Gulf middle-power assertiveness reflects a changed way of exercising American power and room for manoeuvre, not a transfer of power, and real autonomy would require an indigenous military-industrial base the region does not yet have.
recommendations: Treat diversification of partners as distinct from strategic autonomy when assessing Gulf states.
Build domestic defence production, localisation and technology-transfer capacity to underpin independent deterrence.
Give operational meaning to collective-defence commitments, such as the Mecca pact's mutual-attack provision, through actual deployment.
brief.turkey: The Mecca pact in which Türkiye participates has so far failed to produce collective military action, which bears directly on how much Ankara can rely on such arrangements in the Gulf.

title: Who Will Be the Next UN Secretary-General?
summary: Seven candidates are vying to succeed António Guterres as the United Nations’ tenth leader since 1946. Who are they, how are they selected, and what challenges will they face in the role?

ai.sum: Seven candidates are competing to succeed António Guterres as UN Secretary-General, with an explainer on selection and challenges.

brief.summary: The authors explain the race to succeed António Guterres as UN Secretary-General, which is expected to be settled between October and December 2026 and take effect January 1, 2027. They describe seven candidates, five of them women, and argue that Latin America's claim to the post is strong under informal regional rotation. They set out how the selection works: nomination, public vision statements and dialogues, Security Council straw polls, then a formal vote requiring nine votes and no veto, followed by General Assembly appointment. They note the Charter sets no gender or term rules and that no fallback exists if no choice is made by year-end, though past close calls are cited. The authors frame the next holder's agenda around Security Council paralysis, a liquidity crisis, the UN80 reform drive, US funding cuts, and rising security priorities among member states.
brief.argument: The next Secretary-General will be chosen through a largely unchanged, opaque process while inheriting an organisation facing deep funding, reform and Security Council deadlock problems.

title: Bypassing the Pharma Chokepoint
summary: Introduction Over the last twenty years, China has emerged as the United States and Europe’s [PDF] most important foreign source of upstream inputs of critical medicines—namely, key starting materials (KSMs) and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). As U.S. and EU regulators and media more heavily scrutinized API and KSM production, a process that often involves chemical […]

ai.sum: A CFR report examines China's dominance as a source of pharmaceutical starting materials and APIs for the US and Europe.

brief.summary: The authors argue that China has become the main foreign source of key starting materials and active pharmaceutical ingredients for antibiotics, sedatives and emergency drugs supplied to the United States and Europe, and that it now also leads in many late-stage monoclonal antibody programs and is rising in synthetic biology. They frame this as deliberate Chinese industrial policy that creates a dangerous chokepoint, since China has shown willingness to restrict exports to Japan and to undercut India's suppliers. Their remedy is coordinated transatlantic action rather than uncoordinated protectionism. They build on existing steps such as the 2019 US-EU mutual recognition agreement for inspections, the Biopharmaceutical Alliance and the EU Critical Medicines Act. They propose tiered policies depending on how strained or stabilised the transatlantic relationship is, from expedited mutual recognition and supply-chain disclosure to joint stockpiles and NATO-linked purchasing. They also flag drug pricing as the main obstacle to cooperation.
brief.argument: Heavy Chinese dominance of upstream pharmaceutical inputs and biotech is a structural security risk that the United States and Europe can only reduce through coordinated, sustained transatlantic cooperation.
recommendations: Create mutual regulatory recognition for GMP-compliant API suppliers, with expedited market-entry pathways in both directions.
Standardise supply-chain disclosure requirements so that concentrations of KSM production, including transshipped material, can be identified.
Build joint stockpiles, joint purchase commitments and crisis allocation rules for prioritised KSMs and APIs.
Use NATO as a platform for joint purchasing of synthetic DNA products for defence and preparedness uses.

summary: The path ahead for either candidate in Israel's election to form a working coalition is uncertain. We polled our experts on what comes next. The post Fast Thinking: How the Israeli election deadlock could end appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council experts polled on how Israel's election deadlock could be resolved and which coalition path is likely.

brief.summary: The authors, three Atlantic Council experts, examine the deadlock after Israel's election, in which neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Gadi Eisenkot's bloc is poised to reach the 61 seats needed for a government. Dan Shapiro reads the result as a clear majority of Israelis wanting a different government, with Netanyahu's coalition falling from 68 to a projected 53 seats. Gina Abercrombie-Winstanley disagrees, arguing Netanyahu has not been thoroughly repudiated, since Likud will be the largest Knesset party, and that the backlash reflects Israel writ large rather than one leader. Shalom Lipner stresses the roughly 80 percent turnout as a sign of confidence in democracy but limited trust in representatives. The authors see Netanyahu's best route as recruiting opposition members, while Eisenkot's route is harder because it depends on Arab parties, which many opposition members reject. They expect President Herzog to push for a unity government, though calls for it have so far met resistance, and they raise the possibility of another election in about six months.
brief.argument: The election produced a deadlock that neither leading bloc can easily break, and the route to a government runs through difficult choices on coalition partners, Arab parties and a possible unity government.

title: What’s Behind the Protests and Riots in France, and What Comes Next
summary: Massive protests have swept across France since mid-September as students have rallied against the country’s education system and rising living costs. But the chaos could be a boon for France’s more extreme parties before next year’s elections.

ai.sum: Mass protests across France since mid-September over education and living costs may boost extreme parties before next year's elections.

brief.summary: The authors trace France's school protests, which began at a Créteil high school in September, to chronic problems: overcrowded classes, unfilled teacher posts, decaying and overheated buildings, falling PISA scores and the complex Parcoursup admissions platform. They argue the movement widened into anger over cost of living, a generational imbalance in spending (roughly a third of the education budget goes to pensions) and distrust of government. They describe a violent escalation on October 17, with mass arrests and looting, and a government response of substitute teachers, dropped tuition plans and promised Parcoursup changes. The authors contend the disorder helps Marine Le Pen's National Rally cast itself as the party of law and order, while Mélenchon's far left gains among young voters, so the April 2027 election could pit the two extremes against each other. They see Macron as weakened and a lame duck facing a debt crisis.
brief.argument: The French school protests reflect structural education and generational grievances, but the violence is reshaping the 2027 presidential race in favour of the political extremes.
recommendations: Replace Parcoursup by 2028, with interim changes by 2027, as the government has proposed.
Address teacher shortages through pay and recruitment, given stagnant salaries and physical threats against staff.
Renovate school buildings and add cooling and insulation as heat waves intensify.

title: Canada Shows the Limits of Trump’s Hardball Trade Tactics
summary: Trump’s trade war with Canada assumed economic size would translate into bargaining power. Ottawa’s refusal to back down, and the strain the tariffs are putting on U.S. border states ahead of the midterms, are opening cracks in the administration’s approach.

ai.sum: Ottawa's refusal to back down from US tariffs, and the strain on US border states ahead of the midterms, are exposing limits to Trump's hardball trade approach toward Canada.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Trump's tariff campaign against Canada assumed that the U.S. economy, about ten times larger, would translate into decisive bargaining power. Instead, Canada has shown resilience: its fiscal position lets Ottawa support hit industries, its weak currency offsets tariff costs, and oil revenues cushion the blow. Canadian public opinion backs Prime Minister Carney's refusal to yield, and he is pursuing alternative partners such as Asian markets and EU associate membership. Drawing on Keohane and Nye's interdependence theory and the USMCA talks, the author contends that complex economic ties limit how far Washington can push Canada. Signs of U.S. retreat, including lifted tariffs requested by a vulnerable senator, suggest the strategy is cracking, and the piece frames Canada's stance as a lesson for other countries facing Trump's trade pressure.
brief.argument: Canada's resilience, complex cross-border ties and diversification show that U.S. economic size does not automatically yield bargaining leverage over a smaller partner.
recommendations: Use fiscal space to cushion sectors hit by U.S. tariffs while avoiding capitulation
Diversify trade toward Asia and the EU to reduce dependence on the U.S. market
Leverage cross-border dependencies such as energy, potash, electricity and state-level exports as bargaining chips

Glenny discusses why Vučić conceded within hours, whether this marks the end of his era or a possible comeback, and whether a government of newcomers can run institutions built by the old regime and break ties with organised crime. The conversation also covers Belgrade's likely orientation on EU accession, Russia, Washington and Kosovo, and the possible spillover to Albania after five months of protests. Glenny reports seeing considerable goodwill regionally and in Europe, and argues the new government must decide how to use it. He frames the open question as whether Serbia can credibly move onto the EU accession path.
brief.argument: Glenny argues that the Student List's win is a real opening for Serbia, but that its durability depends on whether newcomers can govern and reform inherited institutions while breaking with organised crime.

brief.argument: Lone-wolf jihadist attacks have not generated the self-sustaining momentum needed to overcome the aggregation problem, though a well-placed individual could still produce strategic effects.

title: Europe’s Defense Dilemma
summary: Fix and Fiott argue that Europe has three options to prepare for a future of limited or conditional U.S. support: It can hope for a more European NATO, develop an EU-based defense union, or create a more flexible European defense coalition of the willing to deter against Russia and absorb future shocks to the transatlantic relationship.

ai.sum: CFR analysis sets out three European options for defence if US support becomes limited: a more European NATO, an EU defence union, or a flexible coalition.

brief.summary: Fix and Fiott argue that Europe must prepare for a future of limited or conditional U.S. support and that Russia will remain the main threat regardless of any Ukraine ceasefire. They set out three models: a more European NATO, in which Europeans take primary responsibility for conventional defence while keeping U.S. nuclear backing; a European defence union built on the EU's mutual-defence and solidarity clauses (TEU Article 42(7) and TFEU Article 222); and a flexible coalition of willing European states including Ukraine. The authors assess each model against deterrence, industrial, legal and financial costs and U.S. interests. They conclude that the likeliest outcome combines all three, with a coalition needing permanent support structures from NATO or the EU, and they stress that the models are complementary rather than exclusive.
brief.argument: Europe should treat a more European NATO, an EU defence union and a flexible defence coalition as complementary options, since none alone can reliably deter Russia without U.S. support.
recommendations: Focus on defence investment, capability development and defence-industrial expansion whichever framework prevails.
Build a durable coalition of willing European states, including Ukraine, to supply the political flexibility a reformed NATO or EU lacks in a crisis.
Pair any coalition with permanent support structures from NATO or the EU.
Make Article 42(7) credible by developing clear response mechanisms and planning architecture.
brief.turkey: Türkiye sits outside the EU's mutual-defence framework but within NATO, so a more European NATO or a coalition-based architecture would directly affect its alliance position, defence-industrial ties with European partners and its role in European security.

title: The Board of Peace for Gaza is not a commercial enterprise. It should stop acting like one.
summary: The Board of Peace is missing the infrastructure, funding, and security guarantees it needs to make progress on its mission. The post The Board of Peace for Gaza is not a commercial enterprise. It should stop acting like one. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council commentary argues the Gaza Board of Peace lacks funding, infrastructure and security guarantees and should stop operating like a commercial enterprise.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Board of Peace, launched in January at Davos, is struggling to turn its political vision for Gaza into working operations. They contend it lacks institutional infrastructure, implementation partners, sufficient financing, and credible security guarantees. They compare it unfavourably with the earlier Gaza Reconstruction Mechanism, which had clear approval roles for all three parties. Funding is stuck in a chicken-and-egg problem: donors wait for a credible mechanism, while the mechanism needs predictable money. Hamas's control of commercial imports and the absence of a deployed security force keep the environment dependent on Israel. The authors hold that the decisive structural gap is the lack of a workable partnership with Israel on access, crossings and security, without which the $71 billion reconstruction plan cannot be executed.
brief.argument: The Board of Peace's reconstruction vision for Gaza will remain undelivered until it builds the institutional, financial, security and practical arrangements with Israel needed to implement it.
recommendations: Establish a practical security and access partnership with Israel covering crossings, movement, imports and infrastructure protection.
Build an independent technical implementation capacity that converts needs assessments into a prioritised, costed programme.
Secure multi-year, predictable financing with transparent procurement and donor coordination.
Staff and deploy the International Stabilization Force and a Palestinian police structure to provide security for reconstruction.
